## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Topological Data Analysis for Imaging and Machine Learning
  Official title       Topological data analysis for imaging and machine learning.
  Instructors          J. TIERNY, F.CHAZAL (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 1 · period 1 (28/09/2026 – 08/01/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 24 h (lectures 12 h, labs 12 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Modelling]{.badge .label} · domains on master-mva.com: Computer Vision
  Language             not displayed on master-mva.com or on the Université Paris-Saclay course detail (the master-mva.com description is written in English)
  Assessment           master-mva.com: “Short lesson exam and research seminar”, with no weights displayed. Université Paris-Saclay course detail: “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (partial continuous assessment).
  Prerequisites        “Admission to MVA. Programming skills in Python and/or C++ are recommended.” (master-mva.com)
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with an M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics who knows linear algebra and some Python, and who wants to measure the shape of data — its components, loops and cavities — in images, scalar fields and point clouds, robustly to noise.

**Empirical first**: a 64 × 64 image of three Gaussian bumps plus Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.05 has 721 local maxima. Persistence gives the two secondary bumps the values 0.734 and 0.64, and every noise peak at most 0.172 (Code 4.2). One threshold in that gap recovers the three objects, and the segmentation that follows finds the three regions of the clean image (Code 6.1). In the same way, 5 % of outliers cut the persistence of the loop of a sampled circle from 0.80 to 0.44, while the distance to a measure keeps 0.63 (Code 7.1).

Topological data analysis (TDA) describes data by the features that survive continuous deformation: connected components, loops, cavities, and the way they appear and disappear across scales. The course builds these descriptors from scratch — simplicial complexes, homology, Morse theory, persistence — and uses them for scientific visualization in 2D and 3D and for machine learning in high dimension. It shares tools with [Geometric Data Analysis](../s1-geometric-data-analysis/index.html), [Geometry Processing and Geometric Deep Learning](../s1-geometry-processing-gdl/index.html) and [Optimal Transport for Machine Learning](../s1-optimal-transport-ml/index.html), whose Wasserstein distances reappear between persistence diagrams.

### What you will be able to do

-   Build Čech, Vietoris–Rips, alpha and lower-star filtrations from point clouds, images and scalar fields, and bound how far the Rips and Čech complexes differ.
-   Compute Betti numbers by Gaussian elimination over the two-element field, and explain when the choice of coefficients matters.
-   Classify the critical points of a piecewise-linear scalar field and check the result against the Euler characteristic.
-   Compute persistence diagrams with the reduction algorithm and with union-find, and compare them with the bottleneck and Wasserstein distances.
-   State and use the stability theorem to separate topological signal from noise and to simplify a scalar field.
-   Compute merge trees, contour trees and Mapper graphs, and relate them to the Reeb graph of a function.
-   Segment an image with the cells of a Morse–Smale complex, simplified by persistence.
-   Infer the homology of a sampled shape with guarantees, and make the inference robust to outliers with the distance to a measure.
-   Cluster data with persistence-based clustering (ToMATo) and choose its parameter from a diagram.
-   Turn persistence diagrams into stable features (landscapes, images, kernels) for classification, and differentiate a topological loss.
-   Choose data structures and algorithms (simplex trees, clearing, cohomology) that make these computations fast, in Python or C++.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com presents topological data analysis [1–6] as a sound family of techniques for the interactive analysis and visualization of data in imaging and machine learning. As acquired or simulated data sets in 2D, 3D and nD grow in size and complexity, these approaches help users understand their data through its topological and geometric structure.

In low dimensions, the description continues, TDA lets users extract, interact with, measure and classify geometric features defined by level sets or integral lines. Simplification based on persistent homology builds multi-scale topological representations that support robust analyses and comparisons despite noise. In higher dimensions, these techniques have been adapted into new clustering algorithms.

The stated purpose is to introduce the main concepts of this recent field and to illustrate their use in imaging (scientific visualization) and machine learning, from a mathematical and a practical point of view, with the Gudhi [7] and TTK [8] libraries. Each item of the official page is matched below.

### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites: admission to the MVA; programming skills in Python and/or C++ are recommended (master-mva.com). The instructors listed on master-mva.com are Frédéric Chazal (INRIA) and Julien Tierny (CNRS). The course is taught in period 1, so only the refreshers come before it.

-   **Refreshers** — [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) for ranks, kernels and quotients (ch. 0, 2, 4); [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) for the sampling and bootstrap arguments of ch. 7; [Scientific Python, NumPy and PyTorch](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) for the labs and the differentiable losses of ch. 8.
-   **Related courses of semester 1** — [Geometric Data Analysis](../s1-geometric-data-analysis/index.html) (intrinsic dimension, neighbourhood graphs), [Geometry Processing and Geometric Deep Learning](../s1-geometry-processing-gdl/index.html) (meshes and Laplacians), [Optimal Transport for Machine Learning](../s1-optimal-transport-ml/index.html) (Wasserstein distances), [Medical Image Analysis](../s1-medical-image-analysis/index.html), [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html) (bootstrap) and [Introduction to Statistical Learning](../s1-intro-statistical-learning/index.html) (the classifiers of ch. 8).
-   **Courses of semester 2 that use its tools** — [Point Clouds and 3D Modelling](../s2-point-clouds-3d/index.html), [Graphs in Machine Learning](../s2-graphs-in-ml/index.html), [Kernel Methods for Machine Learning](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html) (kernels on diagrams), [Geometry and Shape Spaces](../s2-shape-spaces/index.html), [Deformable Models and Geodesic Methods](../s2-deformable-models-geodesics/index.html) (watersheds), [Deep Learning for Medical Imaging](../s2-deep-learning-medical-imaging/index.html) (topological losses for segmentation) and [Algorithms and Learning for Protein Science](../s2-protein-science/index.html).
-   **Afterwards** — the [Research Internship](../s3-research-internship/index.html); ch. 11 lists directions that a first research project can start from.

### Course outline

-   **Review: topology, linear algebra over F2 and union-find** — homotopy equivalence, the Hausdorff distance, ranks over the two-element field, disjoint-set forests.
-   **Simplicial complexes and filtrations** — abstract complexes, nerves, Čech, Rips and alpha complexes, triangulated images, filtrations.
-   **Simplicial homology** — chains, boundaries, Betti numbers by rank, the Euler–Poincaré formula, the role of coefficients.
-   **Smooth and discrete Morse theory** — critical points and cell attachments, piecewise-linear critical points, Banchoff's formula, Forman's discrete gradients.
-   **Persistent homology and persistence diagrams** — persistence modules, the elder rule, the reduction algorithm, bottleneck distance, stability, simplification of images.
-   **Reeb graphs, contour trees and Mapper** — level-set topology, merge trees by union-find, Mapper as a discrete Reeb graph.
-   **Morse–Smale complexes** — integral lines, ascending and descending manifolds, quadrangle cells, watershed segmentation and its simplification.
-   **Topological inference in high dimensions** — reach and sampling theorems, Rips inference and stability, distance to a measure, ToMATo.
-   **Topological signatures and features for learning** — landscapes, persistence images, kernels, learned layers and differentiable persistence.
-   **Implementations in Python and C++** — simplex trees, clearing and cohomology, the Gudhi and TTK libraries, a union-find in C++.
-   **Complements for self-study** — the pairing lemma, interleavings and the isometry theorem, collapses, the nerve theorem, statistics of diagrams.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — multiparameter persistence, statistics and learning, large-scale topological visualization.

### How to study this module

-   Read [ch. 0](#ch0) before session 1. The Hausdorff distance (Proposition 0.3) and union-find (Algorithm 0.6) return in ch. 4, 5, 6 and 7.
-   Follow one thread through the page: the union-find sweep with the elder rule computes connected components (ch. 0), 0-dimensional persistence (ch. 4), merge trees (ch. 5), watershed regions (ch. 6) and ToMATo clusters (ch. 7).
-   After each lab, change one parameter of the code — the noise level, the radius, the threshold, the number of neighbours — and predict the new diagram before running it.
-   Do the exercises listed in the session plan before the next session; read [ch. 10](#ch10) after the session that states each result. The ★★★ exercises and the paper studies of [Projects and assessment](#projects) prepare the research seminar.
-   Python environment: NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and PyTorch on CPU; every block runs in a few seconds. The official labs use Gudhi and TTK; the code here rewrites the needed algorithms in plain Python, so that each step is visible and nothing else must be installed.

## 0. Review: topology, linear algebra over F2 and union-find {#ch0}

Topological data analysis counts features that survive continuous deformation, and it computes them with linear algebra and graph algorithms. This chapter recalls the three M1 tools the course uses everywhere: equivalences of spaces, linear algebra over the two-element field, and the union-find data structure.

### 0.1 Spaces up to deformation

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Homeomorphism, homotopy, deformation retract]{.tag} Let $X, Y$ be topological spaces.

-   A **homeomorphism** is a continuous bijection $h : X \to Y$ with a continuous inverse.
-   Two continuous maps $f, g : X \to Y$ are **homotopic** if there is a continuous $H : X \times [0, 1] \to Y$ with $H(\cdot, 0) = f$ and $H(\cdot, 1) = g$.
-   $X$ and $Y$ are **homotopy equivalent**, written $X \simeq Y$, if there are maps $f : X \to Y$ and $g : Y \to X$ with
    $$
    g \circ f \text{ homotopic to } \mathrm{id}_X \quad \text{and} \quad f \circ g \text{ homotopic to } \mathrm{id}_Y .
    $$
-   $A \subseteq X$ is a **deformation retract** of $X$ if there is a homotopy from $\mathrm{id}_X$ to a map with values in $A$ that fixes $A$ at all times. Then $A \simeq X$.
:::

An annulus deformation retracts onto its middle circle, and a disk onto its centre. A union of small balls around points sampled on a circle is never homeomorphic to the circle, but it can be homotopy equivalent to it. Homotopy equivalence is therefore the right notion for sampled data, and every invariant of this course is a homotopy invariant.

### 0.2 Distances between sets

::: def
[Definition 0.2 — Offsets, Hausdorff and Gromov–Hausdorff distances]{.tag} For a compact set $K \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, the **distance function** is $d_K(x) = \min_{y \in K} \|x - y\|$ and the **offset** of radius $r$ is
$$
K^r = d_K^{-1}([0, r]) = \bigcup_{y \in K} \bar B(y, r).
$$
The **Hausdorff distance** between compact sets $A$ and $B$ is
$$
d_H(A, B) = \inf \{ \varepsilon \geq 0 : A \subseteq B^\varepsilon \text{ and } B \subseteq A^\varepsilon \}.
$$
For two compact metric spaces, the **Gromov–Hausdorff distance** $d_{GH}$ is the infimum of $d_H$ over all isometric embeddings of both spaces into a common metric space.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.3 — Distance functions and the Hausdorff distance]{.tag} For compact sets $A, B \subset \mathbb{R}^d$,
$$
\| d_A - d_B \|_\infty = d_H(A, B).
$$

::: proof
Let $\varepsilon = d_H(A, B)$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$. Take $b \in B$ with $\|x - b\| = d_B(x)$, then $a \in A$ with $\|a - b\| \leq \varepsilon$.

Then $d_A(x) \leq \|x - a\| \leq d_B(x) + \varepsilon$. Exchanging $A$ and $B$ gives $|d_A(x) - d_B(x)| \leq \varepsilon$.

For the converse, let $a \in A$ maximize $d_B$ on $A$. Then $d_A(a) = 0$, so the sup-distance is at least $\max_A d_B$.

Exchanging the roles of the two sets, and noting that the larger of the two maxima is $d_H(A, B)$, concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Every stability result of ch. 4 and ch. 7 starts from this identity: two samples that are close in Hausdorff distance have close distance functions, hence close offsets.

### 0.3 Linear algebra over the two-element field

::: def
[Definition 0.4 — Vector spaces over F2 and quotients]{.tag} The field $\mathbb{F}_2 = \{0, 1\}$ has $1 + 1 = 0$. A vector of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ is a subset of $\{1, \dots, n\}$, and addition is the symmetric difference.

For a subspace $W \subseteq V$, the **quotient** $V / W$ identifies $v$ and $v'$ when $v - v' \in W$. Its dimension is
$$
\dim V / W = \dim V - \dim W .
$$
For a linear map $A : \mathbb{F}_2^n \to \mathbb{F}_2^m$, the rank–nullity theorem holds as over $\mathbb{R}$: $\dim \ker A + \operatorname{rank} A = n$, and Gaussian elimination computes the rank.
:::

::: ex
[Example 0.5 — A rank that depends on the field]{.tag} Consider
$$
A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
Over $\mathbb{R}$, $\det A = 2$ and the rank is 3. Over $\mathbb{F}_2$, the sum of the three columns is zero, and the rank is 2.

Its columns are the three edges of a triangle, written as sets of vertices: ch. 2 reads the relation above as “the boundary of a triangle is a loop”.
:::

### 0.4 Union-find

:::: thm
[Algorithm 0.6 — Union-find (disjoint-set forest)]{.tag} Each element stores a parent pointer; a root is its own parent and represents its set.

1.  **find**$(a)$ follows the pointers from $a$ to its root, and makes the visited nodes point closer to the root (path compression);
2.  **union**$(a, b)$ makes the root of one set point to the root of the other.

With union by rank and path compression, $m$ operations on $n$ elements cost
$$
O\big(m\, \alpha(n)\big),
$$
where $\alpha$ is the inverse Ackermann function, below 5 for any practical $n$ (Tarjan, 1975).
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.7 — Union-find computes connected components]{.tag} Process the edges of a graph one by one, calling union on their endpoints. After each step, two vertices have the same root if and only if a path of processed edges joins them.

::: proof
By induction on the number of processed edges. Initially every vertex is alone. Processing the edge $uv$ merges the sets of $u$ and $v$.

Afterwards, $x$ and $y$ are joined by processed edges if and only if they were already joined, or one is joined to $u$ and the other to $v$. That is exactly the effect of the union on the sets. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In this course, union-find runs on vertices sorted by a function value. The order in which components merge then carries the information: it gives 0-dimensional persistence (ch. 4), merge trees (ch. 5), watershed regions (ch. 6) and clusters (ch. 7).

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   Topological invariants are invariant under homotopy equivalence, which is the right notion for thickened samples.
-   The sup-distance between distance functions equals the Hausdorff distance between the sets (Proposition 0.3).
-   Over $\mathbb{F}_2$, vectors are sets and addition is the symmetric difference; ranks may differ from ranks over $\mathbb{R}$.
-   Union-find maintains connected components in almost constant time per operation.
:::

## 1. Simplicial complexes and filtrations {#ch1}

A computer cannot store a circle, but it can store points, edges and triangles. This chapter defines these combinatorial models, builds them from point clouds and images, and nests them along a scale.

### 1.1 Simplicial complexes

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Simplicial complexes]{.tag} A **geometric $k$-simplex** is the convex hull of $k + 1$ affinely independent points of $\mathbb{R}^d$; the convex hulls of subsets of these points are its **faces**.

An **abstract simplicial complex** on a finite vertex set $V$ is a family $K$ of non-empty subsets of $V$ that contains every non-empty subset of each of its elements. An element of $K$ with $k + 1$ vertices is a **$k$-simplex**.

A **geometric realization** $|K|$ places the vertices in some $\mathbb{R}^N$ so that each $\sigma$ spans a geometric simplex and two simplices meet in a common face or not at all. A complex of dimension $k$ always has one in $\mathbb{R}^{2k+1}$.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — Euler characteristic, star and link]{.tag} If $K$ has $n_k$ simplices of dimension $k$, its **Euler characteristic** is
$$
\chi(K) = \sum_{k \geq 0} (-1)^k\, n_k .
$$
For a vertex $v$, the **star** $\mathrm{St}(v)$ is the set of simplices that contain $v$. The **link** is
$$
\mathrm{Lk}(v) = \{ \tau \in K : v \notin \tau,\ \tau \cup \{v\} \in K \}.
$$
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.3 — Three small complexes]{.tag}

-   The boundary of a tetrahedron has 4 vertices, 6 edges and 4 triangles: $\chi = 4 - 6 + 4 = 2$, the Euler characteristic of the sphere.
-   On a $3 \times 3$ grid with opposite sides identified, cut each square along one diagonal. This gives a torus with 9 vertices, 27 edges and 18 triangles, and $\chi = 0$.
-   In a triangulated surface, the link of an interior vertex is a cycle of edges, and the link of a boundary vertex is a path.
:::

### 1.2 Nerves

::: def
[Definition 1.4 — Nerve of a cover]{.tag} Let $\mathcal{U} = (U_i)_{i \in I}$ be a finite family of sets. Its **nerve** $N(\mathcal{U})$ is the abstract simplicial complex on $I$ whose simplices are the non-empty $J \subseteq I$ with
$$
\bigcap_{j \in J} U_j \neq \emptyset .
$$
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.5 — Nerve theorem]{.tag} Let $\mathcal{U}$ be a finite family of closed convex sets of $\mathbb{R}^d$. Then
$$
|N(\mathcal{U})| \simeq \bigcup_{i \in I} U_i .
$$
The same holds for a finite closed cover of a triangulable space in which every non-empty intersection is contractible (a *good cover*).

::: proof
*Sketch.* Map the barycentric subdivision of the nerve linearly to points chosen in the intersections; convexity keeps the image in the union. Section 10.4 builds the homotopy inverse; Hatcher (2002, Section 4.G) gives the full proof. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 1.3 Čech and Vietoris–Rips complexes

::: def
[Definition 1.6 — Čech and Rips complexes]{.tag} Let $X$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$ and $r \geq 0$.

-   The **Čech complex** $\check C(X, r)$ is the nerve of the closed balls $\bar B(x, r)$, $x \in X$.
-   The **Vietoris–Rips complex** $R(X, r)$ contains every non-empty $\sigma \subseteq X$ of diameter at most $2r$.

The Rips complex makes sense in any metric space. It is a *flag complex*: a set of vertices is a simplex as soon as all its edges are.
:::

By the nerve theorem, since balls are convex,
$$
\check C(X, r) \simeq X^r .
$$
The Čech complex models the offset faithfully, but testing whether $k + 1$ balls intersect needs a smallest enclosing ball; the Rips complex only needs pairwise distances.

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.7 — Rips and Čech complexes are interleaved]{.tag} For a finite $X \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ and every $r \geq 0$,
$$
\check C(X, r) \subseteq R(X, r) \subseteq \check C\Big(X, \sqrt{\tfrac{2d}{d+1}}\; r\Big) \subseteq \check C(X, \sqrt{2}\, r).
$$
In any metric space, $R(X, r) \subseteq \check C(X, 2r)$, with balls of the ambient space.

::: proof
If the balls of radius $r$ around the vertices of $\sigma$ share a point $z$, then any two vertices are at distance at most $2r$ through $z$. Hence $\sigma \in R(X, r)$.

Conversely, let $\sigma$ have diameter $\delta \leq 2r$. Jung's theorem (1901) says that a set of diameter $\delta$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ lies in a ball of radius
$$
\delta \sqrt{\frac{d}{2(d+1)}} \;\leq\; r \sqrt{\frac{2d}{d+1}} .
$$
The centre of that ball lies in all the balls of this radius around the vertices of $\sigma$.

In a general metric space, any vertex of $\sigma$ lies in all the balls of radius $2r$ around the vertices. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key result — Rips is sandwiched between two Čech complexes]{.tag}
$$
\check C(X, r) \subseteq R(X, r) \subseteq \check C(X, \sqrt{2}\, r)
$$
:::

The constant of Jung's theorem is reached: for the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 1, the Rips triangle appears at $r = 1/2$ and the Čech triangle at the circumradius $1/\sqrt 3$, a ratio of $1.155$ (Exercise 2).

::: ex
[Code 1.1 — Čech and Rips triangles of a sampled circle]{.tag} Thirty points are sampled near the unit circle. For several radii, the code counts the edges and the triangles of both complexes, and checks the inclusion of Theorem 1.7 in the plane.

```python
import numpy as np
from itertools import combinations

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
theta = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, 30)                     # 30 points near the unit circle
P = np.c_[np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)] + 0.05 * rng.normal(size=(30, 2))
D = np.linalg.norm(P[:, None] - P[None], axis=2)

def meb_radius(a, b, c):
    """Radius of the smallest disk containing three points of the plane."""
    ab, bc, ca = np.linalg.norm(a - b), np.linalg.norm(b - c), np.linalg.norm(c - a)
    s = sorted([ab, bc, ca])
    if s[2] ** 2 >= s[0] ** 2 + s[1] ** 2:                 # right or obtuse: half the longest side
        return s[2] / 2
    u, v = b - a, c - a
    area = abs(u[0] * v[1] - u[1] * v[0]) / 2
    return ab * bc * ca / (4 * area)                       # acute: circumradius

triples = list(combinations(range(30), 3))
meb = np.array([meb_radius(*P[list(t)]) for t in triples])
diam = np.array([max(D[i, j], D[i, k], D[j, k]) for i, j, k in triples])
jung = np.sqrt(4 / 3)                                      # sqrt(2d/(d+1)) for d = 2
for r in [0.3, 0.6, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0]:
    edges = int((D[np.triu_indices(30, 1)] <= 2 * r).sum())
    cech, rips = int((meb <= r).sum()), int((diam <= 2 * r).sum())
    ok = np.all(meb[diam <= 2 * r] <= jung * r + 1e-12)   # Rips(r) inside Cech(1.155 r)
    print(f"r = {r:.1f}: edges {edges:3d}, Cech triangles {cech:4d}, "
          f"Rips triangles {rips:4d}, Rips(r) in Cech({jung:.3f} r): {ok}")
```

Up to $r = 0.8$ both complexes have the same triangles (1171 at $r = 0.8$). At $r = 0.9$ the Rips complex has 1848 triangles and the Čech complex 1800; at $r = 1$, 3743 against 3617. The inclusion check prints `True` every time.
:::

The 48 extra triangles at $r = 0.9$ are acute triangles spanning the circle. An inscribed equilateral triangle has side $\sqrt 3$: the Rips complex fills it from $r = 0.866$, the Čech complex only from its circumradius $r = 1$. The Rips complex closes the hole earlier, which ch. 4 measures as the death of a loop.

### 1.4 Alpha complexes and triangulated images

::: def
[Definition 1.8 — Delaunay and alpha complexes]{.tag} The **Voronoi cell** of $x \in X$ is the set of points of $\mathbb{R}^d$ at least as close to $x$ as to any other point of $X$. The **Delaunay complex** is the nerve of the Voronoi cells.

The **alpha complex** $A(X, r)$ is the nerve of the sets $\bar B(x, r) \cap V_x$, where $V_x$ is the Voronoi cell of $x$.
:::

These sets are convex with union $X^r$, so $A(X, r) \simeq X^r$ by the nerve theorem. In general position, the alpha complex is a subcomplex of the Delaunay triangulation: $O(n)$ simplices in the plane, against up to $2^n$ for the Čech complex.

::: def
[Definition 1.9 — Triangulated grids]{.tag} An image or a 2D scalar field is sampled on a grid of $n \times m$ pixels. The **Freudenthal triangulation** has the pixels as vertices, the horizontal, vertical and one family of diagonal edges, and two triangles per square.

With periodic boundary conditions and $n, m \geq 3$, it triangulates the torus with $nm$ vertices, $3nm$ edges and $2nm$ triangles, so $\chi = 0$. Each vertex then has degree 6, and its link is a hexagon.
:::

In 3D, each cube is cut into six tetrahedra; cubical complexes, which keep squares and cubes, are the other common choice.

### 1.5 Filtrations

::: def
[Definition 1.10 — Filtrations and filtration functions]{.tag} A **filtration** of a finite complex $K$ is a family of subcomplexes $(K_r)_{r \in \mathbb{R}}$ with $K_r \subseteq K_s$ whenever $r \leq s$.

It is given by a **filtration function** $f : K \to \mathbb{R}$ that is monotone, that is $f(\tau) \leq f(\sigma)$ whenever $\tau \subseteq \sigma$, through
$$
K_r = \{ \sigma \in K : f(\sigma) \leq r \}.
$$
:::

The Čech, Rips and alpha complexes form filtrations as $r$ grows; for the Rips complex, $f(\sigma)$ is half the diameter of $\sigma$. For scalar fields, the central example is the following.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.11 — Lower-star filtrations]{.tag} Let $f$ be defined on the vertices of $K$, and set
$$
f(\sigma) = \max_{v \in \sigma} f(v).
$$
This function is monotone, and $K_r$ is the subcomplex spanned by the vertices with $f(v) \leq r$. If $f$ is extended linearly on each simplex, the sublevel set of the extension at level $r$ deformation retracts onto $|K_r|$.

::: proof
A face has fewer vertices to maximize over, and a simplex enters $K_r$ when all its vertices do. For the retraction, push each point of a simplex away from the face spanned by its high vertices, along a straight line, onto the face of its low vertices; $f$ decreases along the way (Edelsbrunner and Harer, 2010, Chapter VI). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Superlevel sets use the **upper-star** filtration, with $\min$ instead of $\max$ and the order reversed.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   A simplicial complex is a finite family of vertex sets closed under subsets; its Euler characteristic is the alternating count of simplices.
-   By the nerve theorem, the Čech complex of a point cloud is homotopy equivalent to the union of balls.
-   The Rips complex only uses pairwise distances, and it is sandwiched between two Čech complexes (Theorem 1.7).
-   Alpha complexes are smaller; images become triangulated grids; scalar fields give lower-star filtrations.
:::

## 2. Simplicial homology {#ch2}

Homology counts the holes of a complex in each dimension — components, loops, cavities — by linear algebra on its simplices. This chapter defines it over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and computes it by Gaussian elimination.

### 2.1 Chains, cycles and boundaries

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Chains and the boundary map]{.tag} The space of **$k$-chains** $C_k(K)$ is the $\mathbb{F}_2$-vector space with one basis vector per $k$-simplex: a chain is a set of $k$-simplices, and the sum is the symmetric difference.

The **boundary** of a $k$-simplex is the sum of its $(k-1)$-faces,
$$
\partial_k [v_0, \dots, v_k] = \sum_{i=0}^{k} [v_0, \dots, \widehat{v_i}, \dots, v_k],
$$
where the hat removes a vertex. It extends linearly to $\partial_k : C_k \to C_{k-1}$, with $\partial_0 = 0$.
:::

For a triangle, $\partial [a, b, c] = ab + bc + ca$, and the boundary of this loop is $(a + b) + (b + c) + (c + a) = 0$. This is general.

:::: thm
[Lemma 2.2 — The boundary of a boundary is zero]{.tag}
$$
\partial_{k-1} \circ \partial_k = 0 .
$$

::: proof
Let $\sigma$ be a $k$-simplex. Each $(k-2)$-face of $\sigma$ is obtained by removing two of its vertices, in two possible orders. It therefore appears twice in $\partial \partial \sigma$, and twice is zero in $\mathbb{F}_2$. Linearity concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 2.3 — Homology and Betti numbers]{.tag} The **cycles** are $Z_k = \ker \partial_k$ and the **boundaries** are $B_k = \operatorname{im} \partial_{k+1}$. By Lemma 2.2, $B_k \subseteq Z_k$. The **$k$-th homology group** and the **Betti number** are
$$
H_k(K) = Z_k / B_k, \qquad \beta_k = \dim H_k(K).
$$
:::

A $k$-cycle that is not a boundary encloses a $k$-dimensional hole; two cycles are *homologous* when their difference bounds.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.4 — Betti numbers by ranks]{.tag} With $n_k$ the number of $k$-simplices,

::: key
[Key result — Betti numbers from two ranks]{.tag}
$$
\beta_k = n_k - \operatorname{rank} \partial_k - \operatorname{rank} \partial_{k+1}
$$
:::

::: proof
By Definition 0.4, $\beta_k = \dim Z_k - \dim B_k$. By rank–nullity, $\dim Z_k = n_k - \operatorname{rank} \partial_k$, and $\dim B_k = \operatorname{rank} \partial_{k+1}$ by definition. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 2.2 First computations

::: ex
[Example 2.5 — Circle, disk and sphere]{.tag}

-   *Hollow triangle* (3 vertices, 3 edges). The matrix of $\partial_1$ is the matrix of Example 0.5, of rank 2 over $\mathbb{F}_2$. Hence $\beta_0 = 3 - 0 - 2 = 1$ and $\beta_1 = 3 - 2 - 0 = 1$: one component, one loop.
-   *Filled triangle*. Add the 2-simplex: $\operatorname{rank} \partial_2 = 1$, so $\beta_1 = 0$ and $\beta_2 = 1 - 1 = 0$. The loop now bounds.
-   *Boundary of a tetrahedron* (4, 6, 4 simplices). The ranks are $\operatorname{rank} \partial_1 = 3$ and $\operatorname{rank} \partial_2 = 3$, so the Betti numbers are $(1, 0, 1)$: one cavity, as for a sphere.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.6 — $\beta_0$ counts connected components]{.tag} $\beta_0$ is the number of connected components of the graph formed by the vertices and edges of $K$.

::: proof
In $H_0 = C_0 / B_0$, two vertices $u, v$ are equal when $u + v$ is a boundary. If a path $u = w_0, \dots, w_\ell = v$ exists, $u + v$ is the boundary of the sum of its edges, by telescoping.

Conversely, a sum of edges has an even number of endpoints in each component. So $u + v$ is a boundary only if $u$ and $v$ lie in the same component. One vertex per component therefore gives a basis of $H_0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.7 — Euler–Poincaré formula]{.tag}
$$
\chi(K) = \sum_k (-1)^k\, n_k = \sum_k (-1)^k\, \beta_k .
$$

::: proof
Sum Proposition 2.4 with signs. Each $\operatorname{rank} \partial_k$ appears twice, once in $\beta_k$ and once in $\beta_{k-1}$, with opposite signs; the sum telescopes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The torus of Example 1.3 has $\chi = 0$, and Code 2.1 finds $\beta = (1, 2, 1)$: two independent loops and one cavity.

### 2.3 Maps and invariance

::: def
[Definition 2.8 — Simplicial maps and contiguity]{.tag} A **simplicial map** $\varphi : K \to L$ sends vertices to vertices and simplices to simplices; it induces linear maps $C_k(K) \to C_k(L)$ that commute with $\partial$, hence maps $\varphi_* : H_k(K) \to H_k(L)$.

Two simplicial maps $\varphi, \psi : K \to L$ are **contiguous** if, for every simplex $\sigma$ of $K$, the vertex set $\varphi(\sigma) \cup \psi(\sigma)$ is a simplex of $L$.
:::

A simplex is sent to zero in $C_k(L)$ when its image has fewer vertices. Commutation with $\partial$ makes $\varphi_*$ well defined: cycles go to cycles and boundaries to boundaries.

::: thm
[Theorem 2.9 — Invariance]{.tag}

1.  If $|K| \simeq |L|$, then $H_k(K) \cong H_k(L)$ for every $k$: homology is a homotopy invariant of the realization.
2.  Contiguous simplicial maps induce the same map on homology.

The first statement is proved through singular homology (Hatcher, 2002, Corollary 2.11 and Theorem 2.27; Munkres, 1984, Chapter 2). The second follows from a chain homotopy built on the simplices $\varphi(\sigma) \cup \psi(\sigma)$ (Munkres, 1984, Chapter 1).
:::

With the nerve theorem, the homology of the Čech complex is the homology of the union of balls. Contiguity is the tool of the stability proof for Rips filtrations in ch. 7.

### 2.4 Other coefficients

Over $\mathbb{Q}$ or $\mathbb{Z}$, simplices are ordered, and faces receive signs:
$$
\partial [v_0, \dots, v_k] = \sum_{i=0}^{k} (-1)^i\, [v_0, \dots, \widehat{v_i}, \dots, v_k].
$$
Lemma 2.2 still holds, because the two copies of each $(k-2)$-face now carry opposite signs (Exercise 9).

The Betti numbers can depend on the field. On the projective plane, a loop that goes around twice bounds, but the loop itself does not: over $\mathbb{Z}$, $H_1$ is $\mathbb{Z}/2$. Over $\mathbb{F}_2$ this torsion is visible as $\beta_1 = 1$, and over $\mathbb{Q}$ it disappears.

Over $\mathbb{F}_2$ no orientation is needed and each column of a boundary matrix is a set of indices. TDA software therefore works over $\mathbb{F}_2$ or a small prime field.

::: ex
[Code 2.1 — Betti numbers of a torus and a projective plane]{.tag} The code builds all faces of a list of triangles, assembles the boundary matrices, and computes the Betti numbers with Proposition 2.4: over $\mathbb{F}_2$ by Gaussian elimination, over $\mathbb{Q}$ with signed matrices.

```python
import numpy as np
from itertools import combinations

def closure(top):
    """All faces of a list of top simplices, sorted by dimension."""
    faces = {tuple(sorted(f)) for s in top for k in range(1, len(s) + 1)
             for f in combinations(s, k)}
    return [sorted(f for f in faces if len(f) == k + 1) for k in range(len(top[0]))]

def boundary(S, k, signed):
    """Matrix of the boundary map C_k -> C_{k-1} (rows: (k-1)-faces)."""
    index = {f: i for i, f in enumerate(S[k - 1])}
    B = np.zeros((len(S[k - 1]), len(S[k])), dtype=np.int64)
    for j, s in enumerate(S[k]):
        for i in range(len(s)):
            B[index[s[:i] + s[i + 1:]], j] = (-1) ** i if signed else 1
    return B

def rank_f2(B):
    """Rank over Z/2 by Gaussian elimination."""
    A, r = B.copy() % 2, 0
    for c in range(A.shape[1]):
        piv = np.nonzero(A[r:, c])[0]
        if len(piv) == 0:
            continue
        A[[r, r + piv[0]]] = A[[r + piv[0], r]]
        rows = np.nonzero(A[:, c])[0]
        A[rows[rows != r]] ^= A[r]
        r += 1
        if r == A.shape[0]:
            break
    return r

def betti(top, field):
    S = closure(top)
    rk = [0] + [rank_f2(boundary(S, k, False)) if field == "F2"
                else np.linalg.matrix_rank(boundary(S, k, True).astype(float))
                for k in range(1, len(S))] + [0]
    return [int(len(S[k]) - rk[k] - rk[k + 1]) for k in range(len(S))]

n = 3                                    # 3 x 3 periodic grid: a 9-vertex torus
v = lambda i, j: (i % n) * n + (j % n)
torus = [t for i in range(n) for j in range(n) for t in
         [(v(i, j), v(i + 1, j), v(i + 1, j + 1)), (v(i, j), v(i, j + 1), v(i + 1, j + 1))]]
rp2 = [(0, 1, 3), (0, 1, 5), (0, 2, 4), (0, 2, 5), (0, 3, 4),
       (1, 2, 3), (1, 2, 4), (1, 4, 5), (2, 3, 5), (3, 4, 5)]   # 6-vertex projective plane
for name, top in [("torus", torus), ("projective plane", rp2)]:
    S = closure(top)
    chi = sum((-1) ** k * len(S[k]) for k in range(3))
    print(f"{name:16s} f-vector {[len(s) for s in S]}, chi = {chi}, "
          f"Betti over F2 {betti(top, 'F2')}, over Q {betti(top, 'Q')}")
```

The torus has f-vector $(9, 27, 18)$, $\chi = 0$ and Betti numbers $(1, 2, 1)$ over both fields.

The projective plane has f-vector $(6, 15, 10)$ and $\chi = 1$. Its Betti numbers are $(1, 1, 1)$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and $(1, 0, 0)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$: in both cases the alternating sum is the Euler characteristic, as Theorem 2.7 requires.
:::

Gaussian elimination on $n$ simplices costs $O(n^3)$ operations in the worst case. Ch. 4 reorganises this elimination so that one pass over a filtration gives the homology of every subcomplex at once.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   Chains are sets of simplices; the boundary map satisfies $\partial \circ \partial = 0$.
-   $H_k = Z_k / B_k$, and $\beta_k$ follows from the ranks of two boundary matrices (Proposition 2.4).
-   $\beta_0$ counts components, $\beta_1$ independent loops, $\beta_2$ cavities; their alternating sum is $\chi$.
-   Homology is a homotopy invariant, and contiguous maps induce the same map on it.
-   Over $\mathbb{F}_2$ no orientation is needed; coefficients matter only in the presence of torsion.
:::

## 3. Smooth and discrete Morse theory {#ch3}

A scalar field changes the topology of its sublevel sets only at critical points. Morse theory makes this precise; its piecewise-linear and discrete versions turn it into algorithms.

### 3.1 Smooth Morse theory

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Morse functions and index]{.tag} Let $M$ be a closed smooth manifold of dimension $d$ and $f : M \to \mathbb{R}$ smooth. A point $p$ is **critical** if $df(p) = 0$, and **non-degenerate** if moreover the Hessian there is invertible.

The **index** $\lambda(p)$ is the number of negative eigenvalues of the Hessian. $f$ is a **Morse function** if all its critical points are non-degenerate and have distinct values.
:::

Minima have index 0 and maxima index $d$; on a surface, saddles have index 1. Morse functions are dense among smooth functions, so a generic field is Morse.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.2 — Morse lemma and cell attachment]{.tag} Write $M_a = f^{-1}(-\infty, a]$.

1.  Near a non-degenerate critical point $p$ of index $\lambda$, there are coordinates in which
    $$
    f = f(p) - x_1^2 - \dots - x_\lambda^2 + x_{\lambda+1}^2 + \dots + x_d^2 .
    $$
2.  If $f^{-1}([a, b])$ contains no critical point, $M_a$ is a deformation retract of $M_b$.
3.  If $p$ is the only critical point with value in $[c - \varepsilon, c + \varepsilon]$, then $M_{c+\varepsilon}$ is homotopy equivalent to $M_{c-\varepsilon}$ with one cell of dimension $\lambda(p)$ attached.

::: proof
*Sketch* (Milnor, 1963, Lemma 2.2 and Theorems 3.1 and 3.2). For (2), the flow of $-\nabla f / \|\nabla f\|^2$ decreases $f$ at unit speed and pushes $M_b$ onto $M_a$. For (3), in the coordinates of (1), the sublevel set gains a thickened $\lambda$-disk along the negative directions, glued along its boundary sphere. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 3.3 — The height function on a torus]{.tag} Stand a torus vertically and let $f$ be the height. It has four critical points: a minimum, two saddles, a maximum.

The sublevel sets are successively a disk (after the minimum), a cylinder (after the first saddle attaches a 1-cell), a torus minus a disk (after the second saddle) and the torus (after the maximum attaches a 2-cell).
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.4 — Morse inequalities]{.tag} Let $m_\lambda$ be the number of critical points of index $\lambda$ of a Morse function on $M$. Then $m_\lambda \geq \beta_\lambda(M)$ for every $\lambda$, and
$$
\sum_\lambda (-1)^\lambda\, m_\lambda = \chi(M).
$$

::: proof
*Euler formula.* By Theorem 3.2, $M$ is homotopy equivalent to a CW complex with $m_\lambda$ cells of dimension $\lambda$. The Euler characteristic of a CW complex is the alternating count of its cells, and Theorem 2.7 extends to cell complexes.

*Inequalities.* Attaching a $\lambda$-cell changes one Betti number by one: it raises $\beta_\lambda$ or lowers $\beta_{\lambda-1}$. To reach $\beta_\lambda(M)$, at least $\beta_\lambda(M)$ cells of dimension $\lambda$ are needed. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For the torus, $1 - 2 + 1 = 0 = \chi$, and $m = (1, 2, 1)$ equals the Betti numbers: the height function is *perfect*.

### 3.2 Piecewise-linear Morse theory

Data come as values on the vertices of a triangulation, extended linearly. Ties are broken by the vertex index (simulation of simplicity, Edelsbrunner and Mücke, 1990), so all values are distinct.

::: def
[Definition 3.5 — Lower link and PL critical points]{.tag} The **lower link** of a vertex $v$ is the subcomplex of its link spanned by the vertices of lower value:
$$
\mathrm{Lk}^-(v) = \{ \tau \in \mathrm{Lk}(v) : f(u) < f(v) \text{ for all } u \in \tau \}.
$$
The **upper link** is defined with $f(u) > f(v)$. On a triangulated surface, where the link is a cycle, $v$ is:

-   a **minimum** if $\mathrm{Lk}^-(v)$ is empty, a **maximum** if $\mathrm{Lk}^-(v)$ is the whole link;
-   **regular** if $\mathrm{Lk}^-(v)$ is one arc;
-   a **saddle of multiplicity** $k - 1$ if $\mathrm{Lk}^-(v)$ has $k \geq 2$ arcs (a monkey saddle for $k = 3$).
:::

This classification follows Banchoff (1967): entering $v$ adds a cone over $\mathrm{Lk}^-(v)$, which merges $k$ fronts when the lower link has $k$ arcs.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.6 — Banchoff's index formula]{.tag} For a function with distinct values on the vertices of any finite simplicial complex $K$,
$$
\sum_{v} \Big( 1 - \chi\big(\mathrm{Lk}^-(v)\big) \Big) = \chi(K).
$$

::: proof
Each simplex $\sigma$ has a unique highest vertex $v$. Removing $v$ leaves either nothing, when $\sigma = \{v\}$, or a simplex $\tau$ all of whose vertices are lower than $v$.

Such a $\tau$ lies in $\mathrm{Lk}^-(v)$. Conversely, every simplex of the lower link, joined with $v$, is a simplex of $K$ with highest vertex $v$.

Group the terms of $\chi(K)$ by highest vertex. The contribution of $v$ is $1$ for the vertex itself, plus $(-1)^{\dim \tau + 1}$ for each $\tau$ in the lower link:
$$
\chi(K) = \sum_v \Big( 1 - \sum_{\tau \in \mathrm{Lk}^-(v)} (-1)^{\dim \tau} \Big) = \sum_v \big( 1 - \chi(\mathrm{Lk}^-(v)) \big).
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

On a surface, the term $1 - \chi(\mathrm{Lk}^-(v))$ of a vertex is:

-   1 for a minimum (empty lower link) and for a maximum (a cycle, of Euler characteristic 0);
-   0 for a regular vertex (an arc, of Euler characteristic 1);
-   $1 - k$ for a saddle with $k$ lower arcs.

Hence:

::: prop
[Corollary 3.7 — Critical points on a surface]{.tag} Counting each saddle with its multiplicity,
$$
\#\text{minima} - \#\text{saddles} + \#\text{maxima} = \chi(K).
$$
:::

::: ex
[Code 3.1 — Critical points of a noisy field on a torus]{.tag} The field $\cos 2\pi x + \cos 2\pi y$ is sampled on a $64 \times 64$ periodic grid with the Freudenthal triangulation of Definition 1.9, with and without Gaussian noise. The code walks around the hexagonal link of each vertex, counts the lower arcs, and checks Corollary 3.7 with $\chi = 0$.

```python
import numpy as np

def critical_points(f):
    """PL critical vertices of f on the Freudenthal triangulation of a periodic grid.
    Ties are broken by the vertex index (simulation of simplicity)."""
    n, m = f.shape
    key = f.ravel().argsort().argsort().reshape(n, m)       # rank of each vertex = total order
    ring = [(1, 0), (1, 1), (0, 1), (-1, 0), (-1, -1), (0, -1)]  # cyclic link of a vertex
    low = np.stack([np.roll(key, (-di, -dj), axis=(0, 1)) < key for di, dj in ring])
    arcs = (low & ~np.roll(low, 1, axis=0)).sum(axis=0)     # number of lower arcs in the hexagon
    n_low = low.sum(axis=0)
    minima, maxima = n_low == 0, n_low == 6
    saddle_mult = np.where(~minima & ~maxima, arcs - 1, 0)  # a k-fold saddle has k lower arcs
    return minima.sum(), saddle_mult.sum(), maxima.sum()

n = 64
x, y = np.meshgrid(np.arange(n) / n, np.arange(n) / n, indexing="ij")
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for noise in [0.0, 0.05, 0.2]:
    f = np.cos(2 * np.pi * x) + np.cos(2 * np.pi * y) + noise * rng.normal(size=(n, n))
    m0, m1, m2 = critical_points(f)
    print(f"noise {noise:.2f}: minima {m0:4d}, saddles {m1:4d}, maxima {m2:4d}, "
          f"m0 - m1 + m2 = {m0 - m1 + m2}")
```

Without noise, the code finds 1 minimum, 2 saddles and 1 maximum. With noise 0.05 it finds 164, 320 and 156; with noise 0.2, 508, 1005 and 497. The alternating sum is 0 every time.
:::

Noise multiplies the critical points by hundreds, while their alternating sum cannot move. Deciding which of them matter is the job of persistence (ch. 4).

### 3.3 Discrete Morse theory

Forman's theory replaces the gradient by a matching between simplices, which suits exact combinatorial algorithms.

::: def
[Definition 3.8 — Discrete Morse functions]{.tag} A function $F$ on the simplices of $K$ is a **discrete Morse function** if, for every $p$-simplex $\sigma$:

-   at most one coface $\tau$ of dimension $p + 1$ has $F(\tau) \leq F(\sigma)$;
-   at most one face $\nu$ of dimension $p - 1$ has $F(\nu) \geq F(\sigma)$.

A simplex is **critical** when both numbers are zero.
:::

::: def
[Definition 3.9 — Discrete gradient vector fields]{.tag} The **gradient** of $F$ is the set $V$ of pairs $(\sigma < \tau)$, of dimensions $p$ and $p + 1$, with $F(\tau) \leq F(\sigma)$. Each simplex belongs to at most one pair, and the unpaired simplices are the critical ones.

A **$V$-path** alternates $\sigma_0 < \tau_0 > \sigma_1 < \tau_1 > \dots$, with $(\sigma_i, \tau_i) \in V$ and $\sigma_{i+1} \neq \sigma_i$ a face of $\tau_i$. A matching is the gradient of some discrete Morse function if and only if it has no closed $V$-path (Forman, 1998).
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 3.10 — Forman's theorem]{.tag} If $F$ is a discrete Morse function on $K$, then $|K|$ is homotopy equivalent to a CW complex with exactly one cell of dimension $p$ for each critical $p$-simplex.

In particular, if $m_p$ counts the critical $p$-simplices, then $m_p \geq \beta_p(K)$ and $\sum_p (-1)^p m_p = \chi(K)$. The proof replaces each gradient pair by an elementary collapse, which does not change the homotopy type (Section 10.3).
:::

::: ex
[Example 3.11 — Gradients on a triangle and on its boundary]{.tag}

-   *Filled triangle* $abc$. The pairs $(b, ab)$, $(c, ac)$ and $(bc, abc)$ leave only $a$ critical: the triangle is contractible.
-   *Hollow triangle*. Pair $b$ with $ab$ and $c$ with $bc$. The vertex $a$ and the edge $ca$ remain critical: one 0-cell and one 1-cell, a circle.
-   On the hollow triangle, the pairs $(a, ab)$, $(b, bc)$ and $(c, ca)$ form a closed $V$-path: they are not a gradient.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.12 — Steepest-descent pairing]{.tag} Let $f$ have distinct values on the vertices. Pair each vertex that is not a local minimum with the edge to its lowest neighbour. This is a discrete gradient, whose critical vertices are the local minima.

::: proof
An edge $vu$ with $f(u) < f(v)$ can only be paired with $v$, so each edge is used at most once. Along a $V$-path $v_0, v_0 v_1, v_1, \dots$, each step goes to a lower vertex, so the values strictly decrease and no path closes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Robins, Wood and Sheppard (2011) extend this pairing to all dimensions, with critical simplices matching the topology changes of the lower-star filtration; their $V$-paths replace integral lines in ch. 6.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   Sublevel sets of a Morse function change only at critical points, by attaching a cell of dimension equal to the index.
-   The Morse inequalities bound the number of critical points below by the Betti numbers; their alternating sum is $\chi$.
-   On triangulated data, the lower link classifies vertices; Banchoff's formula is an exact count by highest vertex.
-   Discrete gradients are acyclic matchings of simplices; critical simplices give a cell complex of the same homotopy type.
:::

## 4. Persistent homology and persistence diagrams {#ch4}

Data come with a scale or a threshold that nobody knows how to choose. Persistence follows every hole across all scales at once, records when it appears and disappears, and summarizes the result stably.

### 4.1 Persistence modules and barcodes

Let $\emptyset = K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \dots \subset K_m = K$ be a filtration in which $K_i$ adds one simplex $\sigma_i$ to $K_{i-1}$ (ties broken arbitrarily).

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Persistence modules and persistent Betti numbers]{.tag} The **persistence module** of degree $k$ is the sequence
$$
H_k(K_0) \to H_k(K_1) \to \dots \to H_k(K_m),
$$
with the maps $\iota_i^j : H_k(K_i) \to H_k(K_j)$ induced by inclusion for $i \leq j$. The **persistent Betti numbers** are
$$
\beta_k^{i,j} = \operatorname{rank} \iota_i^j .
$$
A class $\gamma \in H_k(K_i)$ is **born** at $i$ if it is not in the image of $\iota_{i-1}^{i}$.

It **dies** at $j > i$ if its image in $H_k(K_{j-1})$ is not in the image of $H_k(K_{i-1})$, while its image in $H_k(K_j)$ is: at $j$ it merges with an older class.
:::

$\beta_k^{i,j}$ counts the $k$-dimensional holes of $K_i$ that are still holes in $K_j$.

::: thm
[Theorem 4.2 — Structure theorem]{.tag} A persistence module of finite-dimensional spaces decomposes, uniquely up to order, into a direct sum of **interval modules**: each interval $[b, d)$ contributes a copy of $\mathbb{F}_2$ at the indices $b \leq i < d$, connected by identity maps, and $0$ elsewhere.

The multiset of intervals is the **barcode**. It satisfies, for $i \leq j$,
$$
\beta_k^{i,j} = \#\{ [b, d) \text{ in the barcode} : b \leq i \text{ and } j < d \}.
$$
For finite filtrations this is due to Zomorodian and Carlsson (2005), through graded modules over $\mathbb{F}_2[t]$; Crawley-Boevey (2015) extends it to modules indexed by $\mathbb{R}$ with finite-dimensional spaces.
:::

An interval $[b, d)$ of indices becomes the interval $[f(\sigma_b), f(\sigma_d))$ of scales; intervals of length zero are discarded.

### 4.2 The elder rule

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.3 — 0-dimensional persistence by union-find]{.tag} Sweep the filtration with union-find (Algorithm 0.6). A vertex starts a new component. When an edge joins two components, the **younger** one — whose oldest vertex entered later — dies, and its bar $[b, d)$ goes from the entry of that oldest vertex to the entry of the edge. The oldest component never dies.

The resulting barcode is the barcode of $H_0$.

::: proof
By Proposition 2.6, $\beta_0^{i,j}$ is the number of components of $K_j$ that contain a vertex of $K_i$. Each component $C$ of $K_j$ carries exactly one bar alive at $j$, the bar of its oldest vertex.

$C$ meets $K_i$ if and only if its oldest vertex entered at or before $i$, that is, if and only if this bar starts at or before $i$. So the elder-rule bars satisfy the formula of Theorem 4.2 for all $i \leq j$. The persistent Betti numbers determine the barcode by inclusion–exclusion, which concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For the Rips filtration, the finite $H_0$ bars die at half the edge lengths of a minimum spanning tree: the sweep is Kruskal's algorithm (Exercise 14).

### 4.3 The reduction algorithm

Order the simplices as in the filtration, and let $\partial$ be the $m \times m$ boundary matrix over $\mathbb{F}_2$: column $j$ holds the faces of $\sigma_j$. For a non-zero column, $\mathrm{low}(j)$ is the index of its lowest 1.

:::: thm
[Algorithm 4.4 — Standard reduction]{.tag}

1.  For $j = 1, \dots, m$: while some $j' < j$ has $\mathrm{low}(j') = \mathrm{low}(j)$, add column $j'$ to column $j$.
2.  The result is $R = \partial V$ with $V$ upper triangular and invertible; the non-zero columns of $R$ have distinct lows.

The cost is $O(m^3)$ in the worst case.
::::

::: thm
[Theorem 4.5 — Persistence pairs]{.tag} After the reduction:

-   each non-zero column $j$ with $\mathrm{low}(j) = i$ gives a bar $[f(\sigma_i), f(\sigma_j))$ in degree $\dim \sigma_i$: $\sigma_i$ creates a class that $\sigma_j$ kills;
-   each $i$ with $R_i = 0$ that is the low of no column gives an infinite bar $[f(\sigma_i), \infty)$.

The pairs do not depend on the order of the column additions (*pairing lemma*, Cohen-Steiner, Edelsbrunner and Morozov, 2006). Section 10.1 proves it with ranks of lower-left submatrices.
:::

A simplex with $R_i = 0$ is **positive**: it creates a class. A simplex with $R_j \neq 0$ is **negative**: it kills the youngest class contained in the cycle $R_j$.

::: ex
[Code 4.1 — Persistence of the Rips filtration of a noisy circle]{.tag} The code sorts the simplices of dimension at most 2 of the Rips filtration of the points of Code 1.1, then runs Algorithm 4.4 with columns stored as sets.

```python
import numpy as np
from itertools import combinations

def rips_filtration(P, rmax):
    """Simplices of dimension <= 2 of the Rips filtration, value r = diameter / 2."""
    D = np.linalg.norm(P[:, None] - P[None], axis=2) / 2
    n = len(P)
    S = [((i,), 0.0) for i in range(n)]
    S += [((i, j), D[i, j]) for i, j in combinations(range(n), 2) if D[i, j] <= rmax]
    S += [((i, j, k), max(D[i, j], D[i, k], D[j, k])) for i, j, k in combinations(range(n), 3)
          if max(D[i, j], D[i, k], D[j, k]) <= rmax]
    return sorted(S, key=lambda s: (s[1], len(s[0])))       # faces before cofaces

def persistence(S):
    """Standard column reduction over Z/2; returns (dim, birth, death) triples."""
    index = {s: i for i, (s, _) in enumerate(S)}
    low_of, cols, pairs, paired = {}, [], [], set()
    for j, (s, val) in enumerate(S):
        col = {index[s[:i] + s[i + 1:]] for i in range(len(s))} if len(s) > 1 else set()
        while col and max(col) in low_of:                  # add the column with the same pivot
            col ^= cols[low_of[max(col)]]
        cols.append(col)
        if col:
            i = max(col)
            low_of[i] = j
            paired |= {i, j}
            if val > S[i][1]:                              # skip zero-length intervals
                pairs.append((len(S[i][0]) - 1, S[i][1], val))
    pairs += [(len(s) - 1, val, np.inf) for j, (s, val) in enumerate(S)
              if j not in paired and len(s) < 3]           # essential classes (dim < top)
    return pairs

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
theta = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, 30)
P = np.c_[np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)] + 0.05 * rng.normal(size=(30, 2))
S = rips_filtration(P, rmax=1.2)
dgm = persistence(S)
h1 = sorted([(b, d) for k, b, d in dgm if k == 1], key=lambda p: p[0] - p[1])
print(f"{len(S)} simplices; H0: {sum(k == 0 for k, _, _ in dgm)} intervals, "
      f"H1: {len(h1)} intervals")
for b, d in h1[:3]:
    print(f"H1 interval [{b:.3f}, {d:.3f}), persistence {d - b:.3f}")
```

The filtration has 4525 simplices. The code finds 30 intervals in $H_0$ (29 finite, one infinite) and a single $H_1$ interval of positive length, $[0.317, 0.829)$, of persistence 0.512.
:::

The loop is born when the largest gap between consecutive points closes, and dies near $\sqrt 3 / 2 = 0.866$, when the Rips complex fills an inscribed triangle (Code 1.1).

### 4.4 Persistence diagrams and their distances

::: def
[Definition 4.6 — Persistence diagram]{.tag} The **persistence diagram** $\mathrm{Dgm}_k(f)$ is the multiset of points $(b, d)$, one per bar of degree $k$, with $d = +\infty$ for infinite bars.

It also contains every point of the diagonal $\Delta = \{(t, t)\}$, with infinite multiplicity. The **persistence** of $(b, d)$ is $d - b$.
:::

Points far from the diagonal are long-lived features; the diagonal lets diagrams of different sizes be matched.

::: def
[Definition 4.7 — Bottleneck and Wasserstein distances]{.tag} A **matching** between two diagrams $D$ and $D'$ is a bijection $\gamma : D \to D'$, where points may be matched to the diagonal. The **bottleneck distance** and the **$q$-Wasserstein distance** are
$$
d_B(D, D') = \inf_\gamma \sup_{p \in D} \| p - \gamma(p) \|_\infty, \qquad W_q(D, D') = \inf_\gamma \Big( \sum_{p \in D} \| p - \gamma(p) \|_\infty^q \Big)^{1/q}.
$$
Matching $(b, d)$ to its closest diagonal point costs $(d - b)/2$.
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.8 — Distances by hand]{.tag} Take $D = \{(0, 4), (1, 2)\}$ and $D' = \{(0, 3.5)\}$.

-   Match $(0, 4)$ with $(0, 3.5)$, at cost $0.5$, and send $(1, 2)$ to the diagonal, at cost $0.5$.
-   Matching $(1, 2)$ with $(0, 3.5)$ instead would cost $1.5$.

Hence
$$
d_B(D, D') = 0.5, \qquad W_1(D, D') = 1 .
$$
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 4.9 — Computing the bottleneck distance]{.tag} For finite diagrams with $n$ and $n'$ points, add a diagonal copy of each point of the other diagram, and let any two diagonal copies be matched at cost 0. Then $d_B$ is the smallest threshold $t$ among the pairwise costs for which the bipartite graph of the pairs of cost at most $t$ has a perfect matching.

A binary search over the $O((n + n')^2)$ costs and the Hopcroft–Karp algorithm give $d_B$ in polynomial time; $W_q$ is an assignment problem on the same graph.
:::

### 4.5 Stability

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.10 — Stability of persistence diagrams]{.tag} Let $f, g$ be two monotone filtration functions on the same finite complex $K$, for instance the lower-star filtrations of two images on the same grid. For every degree $k$:

::: key
[Key result — stability]{.tag}
$$
d_B\big( \mathrm{Dgm}_k(f), \mathrm{Dgm}_k(g) \big) \;\leq\; \| f - g \|_\infty
$$
:::

::: proof
*Sketch* (the vineyard argument of Cohen-Steiner, Edelsbrunner and Morozov, 2006). Let $f_t = (1 - t) f + t g$ for $t \in [0, 1]$; each $f_t$ is monotone.

The pairs of Theorem 4.5 depend only on the order of the simplices. Between two times at which this order changes, the paired simplices $(\sigma, \tau)$ are fixed, and the point $(f_t(\sigma), f_t(\tau))$ moves at speed at most $\| g - f \|_\infty$ in the sup norm.

At a time when two simplices swap, they have equal values, and the diagram is continuous across the swap: only points with coinciding coordinates exchange their pairs. Following each point along $[0, 1]$ defines a matching that moves no point by more than $\| f - g \|_\infty$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Cohen-Steiner, Edelsbrunner and Harer (2007) proved it for tame functions on triangulable spaces; Section 10.2 gives the algebraic version.

### 4.6 Images, noise and simplification

For an image, bright blobs are maxima, tracked by superlevel sets. In degree 0, each local maximum dies at the saddle level where it joins a higher peak: its persistence is its **prominence**.

::: ex
[Code 4.2 — Superlevel-set persistence of a noisy image]{.tag} Three Gaussian bumps of heights 1, 0.8 and 0.6 (width 6 pixels) on a $64 \times 64$ grid, plus noise of standard deviation 0.05. Proposition 4.3 runs on the 4-neighbour graph, in decreasing order.

```python
import numpy as np

def superlevel_h0(f):
    """0-dim persistence of the superlevel sets of an image (4-neighbour grid),
    by union-find and the elder rule. Returns (birth, death) pairs, birth >= death."""
    n, m = f.shape
    flat = f.ravel()
    parent = -np.ones(n * m, dtype=int)                # -1 = pixel not yet in the filtration
    def find(a):
        while parent[a] != a:
            parent[a] = parent[parent[a]]
            a = parent[a]
        return a
    pairs = []
    for v in np.argsort(-flat, kind="stable"):         # decreasing values
        parent[v] = v
        i, j = divmod(v, m)
        for a, b in [(i - 1, j), (i + 1, j), (i, j - 1), (i, j + 1)]:
            if 0 <= a < n and 0 <= b < m and parent[a * m + b] >= 0:
                ru, rv = find(a * m + b), find(v)
                if ru != rv:                           # elder rule: the lower peak dies
                    young, old = (ru, rv) if flat[ru] < flat[rv] else (rv, ru)
                    if flat[young] > flat[v]:          # skip zero-length pairs
                        pairs.append((flat[young], flat[v]))
                    parent[young] = old
    pairs.append((flat.max(), -np.inf))                # the essential class
    return np.array(pairs)

n = 64
x, y = np.meshgrid(np.arange(n), np.arange(n), indexing="ij")
bump = lambda cx, cy, h: h * np.exp(-((x - cx) ** 2 + (y - cy) ** 2) / (2 * 6.0 ** 2))
clean = bump(16, 16, 1.0) + bump(44, 20, 0.8) + bump(30, 48, 0.6)
img = clean + 0.05 * np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=(n, n))
dgm = superlevel_h0(img)
pers = np.sort(dgm[:, 0] - dgm[:, 1])[::-1]
print(f"{len(dgm)} local maxima; five largest persistences: {np.round(pers[:5], 3)}")
print(f"points with persistence > 0.25: {(pers > 0.25).sum()}")
```

The image has 721 local maxima. The five largest persistences are $\infty$ (the highest bump), 0.734, 0.64, 0.172 and 0.152: exactly three points exceed 0.25.
:::

The gap between 0.64 and 0.172 separates objects from noise: by Theorem 4.10, noise of sup-norm $\delta$ only creates points of persistence at most $2\delta$.

::: ex
[Code 4.3 — Stability in practice]{.tag} A noisy signal is perturbed by uniform noise of amplitude $\delta$; the code compares both $H_0$ diagrams with Proposition 4.9.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse import csr_matrix
from scipy.sparse.csgraph import maximum_bipartite_matching

def sublevel_h0(f):
    """Finite 0-dim intervals (birth, death) of the sublevel sets of a 1D signal."""
    parent, pairs = -np.ones(len(f), dtype=int), []
    def find(a):
        while parent[a] != a:
            a = parent[a]
        return a
    for v in np.argsort(f, kind="stable"):
        parent[v] = v
        for u in (v - 1, v + 1):
            if 0 <= u < len(f) and parent[u] >= 0:
                ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
                if ru != rv:
                    young, old = (ru, rv) if f[ru] > f[rv] else (rv, ru)
                    if f[young] < f[v]:
                        pairs.append((f[young], f[v]))
                    parent[young] = old
    return np.array(pairs).reshape(-1, 2)

def bottleneck(A, B):
    """Bottleneck distance between finite diagrams, by thresholded bipartite matching.
    Rows: points of A, then diagonal copies of B; columns: points of B, then copies of A."""
    a, b = len(A), len(B)
    C = np.full((a + b, b + a), np.inf)
    C[:a, :b] = np.abs(A[:, None, :] - B[None, :, :]).max(axis=2)
    C[np.arange(a), b + np.arange(a)] = (A[:, 1] - A[:, 0]) / 2   # A_i to the diagonal
    C[a + np.arange(b), np.arange(b)] = (B[:, 1] - B[:, 0]) / 2   # diagonal to B_j
    C[a:, b:] = 0.0                                                # diagonal to diagonal
    values = np.unique(C[np.isfinite(C)])
    lo, hi = 0, len(values) - 1
    while lo < hi:                                     # smallest threshold with a perfect matching
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        match = maximum_bipartite_matching(csr_matrix(C <= values[mid]), perm_type="column")
        lo, hi = (mid + 1, hi) if (match < 0).any() else (lo, mid)
    return values[lo]

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
t = np.linspace(0, 1, 400)
f = np.sin(6 * np.pi * t) + 0.1 * rng.normal(size=t.size)
for delta in [0.01, 0.05, 0.2]:
    g = f + rng.uniform(-delta, delta, size=t.size)
    Df, Dg = sublevel_h0(f), sublevel_h0(g)
    big = [(D[:, 1] - D[:, 0] > 1.5).sum() for D in (Df, Dg)]
    print(f"|f - g|_inf = {np.abs(f - g).max():.4f}: bottleneck = {bottleneck(Df, Dg):.4f}; "
          f"{len(Df)} and {len(Dg)} points, persistence > 1.5: {big[0]} and {big[1]}")
```

For perturbations of sup-norm 0.0100, 0.0500 and 0.2000, the bottleneck distances are 0.0100, 0.0490 and 0.1825. The diagrams have 130 to 138 points, but always exactly two finite points of persistence above 1.5.
:::

Removing a point of persistence $p$ needs a perturbation of sup-norm at least $p/2$, its distance to the diagonal. On surfaces this bound is reached.

::: thm
[Theorem 4.11 — Persistence simplification]{.tag} Let $f$ be a function on a triangulated surface and $\delta > 0$. Some $g$ with $\| f - g \|_\infty \leq \delta$ has exactly as many critical points as $f$ has critical points of persistence greater than $2\delta$, counting the essential ones.

By Theorem 4.10, no function within $\delta$ of $f$ has fewer: this lower bound is tight.

See Edelsbrunner, Morozov and Pascucci (2006) and Bauer, Lange and Wardetzky (2012); Tierny and Pascucci (2012) give the general algorithm used in TTK.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   A persistence module decomposes into intervals: the barcode, or the diagram.
-   In degree 0, union-find with the elder rule computes it; the reduction algorithm does in every degree.
-   Diagrams are compared by matching, with the bottleneck and Wasserstein distances.
-   Stability: $d_B \leq \| f - g \|_\infty$; noise of amplitude $\delta$ only adds points of persistence at most $2\delta$, which simplification removes.
:::

## 5. Reeb graphs, contour trees and Mapper {#ch5}

The level sets of a scalar field split and merge as the level varies. The Reeb graph records this history; Mapper computes a discrete version of it for point clouds.

### 5.1 Reeb graphs

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Reeb graph]{.tag} Let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous. Write $x \sim y$ when $f(x) = f(y)$ and $x, y$ lie in the same connected component of the level set $f^{-1}(f(x))$. The **Reeb graph** is the quotient
$$
R(f) = X / \sim ,
$$
and $f$ induces a function $\bar f$ on it. Each point of $R(f)$ is one connected component of one level set.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — Reeb graphs of Morse functions]{.tag} Let $f$ be a Morse function on a compact connected manifold $X$.

1.  $R(f)$ is a finite graph. Its nodes are the images of the critical points at which the number of components of the level set changes; minima and maxima are nodes of degree 1.
2.  The quotient map induces a surjection on first homology, so $\beta_1(R(f)) \leq \beta_1(X)$.
3.  If $X$ is a closed orientable surface of genus $g$, then $R(f)$ has exactly $g$ independent loops.

See Cole-McLaughlin, Edelsbrunner, Harer, Natarajan and Pascucci (2004) for the third statement, and Dey and Wang (2022, Chapter 7) for the first two.
:::

For the height function of the torus (Example 3.3), the Reeb graph is a minimum, a saddle where the circle splits into two, two parallel arcs, a saddle where they merge, and a maximum: one loop, as $g = 1$.

### 5.2 Merge trees and contour trees

On a simply connected domain, such as a rectangular image, $\beta_1 = 0$, so the Reeb graph is a tree by Theorem 5.2: the **contour tree**.

::: def
[Definition 5.3 — Merge trees]{.tag} The **join tree** of $f$ tracks the components of the superlevel sets $f^{-1}([t, \infty))$ as $t$ decreases: its leaves are the maxima, and its interior nodes are the saddles at which two components join. The **split tree** does the same for sublevel sets and minima.
:::

Both are computed by the union-find sweep of Proposition 4.3, recording a node at every merge. A persistence pair is then a leaf together with the node where its branch meets an older branch: the diagram in degree 0 is the **branch decomposition** of the merge tree (Pascucci, Cole-McLaughlin and Scorzelli, 2004).

::: ex
[Example 5.4 — A split tree by hand]{.tag} Let a path $v_1, \dots, v_7$ carry the values $2, 6, 1, 4, 3, 5, 0$. Sweep upwards:

1.  $v_7$ (0), $v_3$ (1), $v_1$ (2) and $v_5$ (3) are minima: four leaves;
2.  at $v_4$ (4), the components of $v_3$ and $v_5$ meet; the younger one, born at 3, dies: pair $(3, 4)$;
3.  at $v_6$ (5), the components of $v_3$ and $v_7$ meet; the one born at 1 dies: pair $(1, 5)$;
4.  at $v_2$ (6), the component of $v_1$ meets the rest: pair $(2, 6)$.

The split tree has four leaves and three merge nodes, and
$$
\mathrm{Dgm}_0 = \{ (3, 4),\ (1, 5),\ (2, 6),\ (0, \infty) \}.
$$
:::

::: thm
[Algorithm 5.5 — Contour tree from the join and split trees]{.tag} Carr, Snoeyink and Axen (2003) compute the contour tree of a PL function on a simply connected domain in any dimension. They build both merge trees, then repeatedly move to the contour tree a leaf of one tree that satisfies a local degree condition in the other, and delete it from both. The cost is $O(n \log n + N \alpha(N))$ for $n$ vertices and $N$ simplices.
:::

In scientific visualization, an arc of the contour tree is a family of contours without topological change: selecting it segments a feature. Cutting the branch decomposition at a persistence threshold simplifies the tree.

### 5.3 Mapper

::: def
[Definition 5.6 — Mapper]{.tag} Let $X$ be a point cloud, $\varphi : X \to \mathbb{R}$ a **filter** (a coordinate, a density, an eccentricity), and $\mathcal{I}$ a cover of $\varphi(X)$ by overlapping intervals. For each interval $I$, cluster the preimage $\varphi^{-1}(I)$.

The **Mapper graph** (Singh, Mémoli and Carlsson, 2007) is the nerve of the family of all these clusters: one node per cluster, one edge between two clusters that share a point.
:::

When the clusters are connected components and the intervals shrink, Mapper converges to the Reeb graph (Munch and Wang, 2016). Carrière and Oudot (2018) describe which features a given cover keeps, and Carrière, Michel and Oudot (2018) choose the cover from data.

::: ex
[Code 5.1 — Mapper of a circle and of a figure eight]{.tag} Six hundred noisy points are sampled on a circle and on the figure eight $t \mapsto (\sin t, \sin t \cos t)$. The filter is the first coordinate, covered by 8 intervals with 30 % overlap; each preimage is clustered by single linkage at scale 0.25.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import fcluster, linkage

def mapper(X, filt, n_int=8, overlap=0.3, eps=0.25):
    """Mapper graph: cover the range of the filter by overlapping intervals,
    cluster each preimage by single linkage at scale eps, link clusters that share points."""
    lo, hi = filt.min(), filt.max()
    length = (hi - lo) / (n_int - (n_int - 1) * overlap)
    nodes = []
    for k in range(n_int):
        a = lo + k * length * (1 - overlap)
        idx = np.nonzero((filt >= a) & (filt <= a + length))[0]
        if len(idx) == 1:
            nodes.append(set(idx))
        elif len(idx) > 1:
            labels = fcluster(linkage(X[idx], "single"), eps, criterion="distance")
            nodes += [set(idx[labels == c]) for c in np.unique(labels)]
    edges = {(i, j) for i in range(len(nodes)) for j in range(i + 1, len(nodes))
             if nodes[i] & nodes[j]}
    return nodes, edges

def components(n, edges):
    parent = list(range(n))
    def find(a):
        while parent[a] != a:
            a = parent[a]
        return a
    for i, j in edges:
        parent[find(i)] = find(j)
    return len({find(i) for i in range(n)})

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
t = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, 600)
data = {"circle": np.c_[np.cos(t), np.sin(t)],
        "figure eight": np.c_[np.sin(t), np.sin(t) * np.cos(t)]}
for name, X in data.items():
    X = X + 0.03 * rng.normal(size=X.shape)
    nodes, edges = mapper(X, filt=X[:, 0])
    c = components(len(nodes), edges)
    print(f"{name:12s}: {len(nodes)} nodes, {len(edges)} edges, {c} component(s), "
          f"independent loops = {len(edges) - len(nodes) + c}")
```

The circle gives 14 nodes, 14 edges and one loop; the figure eight gives 12 nodes, 13 edges and two loops. The number of loops of a graph is $E - V + C$ (Exercise 10).
:::

Too few intervals merge branches and too little overlap disconnects the graph (Exercise 13). Nicolau, Levine and Carlsson (2011) used Mapper on breast-cancer expression profiles to find a subgroup with excellent survival.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 5

-   The Reeb graph contracts each component of each level set to a point; for Morse functions it is a finite graph with at most $\beta_1(X)$ loops.
-   On simply connected domains it is a tree, the contour tree, built from the join and split trees.
-   Merge trees come from the union-find sweep; their branch decomposition is the 0-dimensional diagram.
-   Mapper is the nerve of clusters of preimages of a filter; it approximates the Reeb graph and depends on the cover.
:::

## 6. Morse–Smale complexes {#ch6}

Following the gradient from every point partitions the domain into cells, each flowing from one minimum to one maximum. These cells segment images along ridges and valleys, and persistence decides which to merge.

### 6.1 Integral lines and cells

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Integral lines, ascending and descending manifolds]{.tag} Let $f$ be a Morse function on a closed Riemannian manifold $M$. An **integral line** is a maximal curve $\gamma$ with
$$
\gamma'(t) = \nabla f(\gamma(t)).
$$
Through each regular point passes exactly one integral line; it starts and ends at critical points.

For a critical point $p$, the **descending manifold** $D(p)$ consists of $p$ and the points whose integral line ends at $p$.

The **ascending manifold** $A(p)$ consists of $p$ and the points whose integral line starts at $p$.
:::

By the stable manifold theorem, if $p$ has index $\lambda$, then $D(p)$ is an open cell of dimension $\lambda$ and $A(p)$ an open cell of dimension $d - \lambda$.

The descending manifolds partition $M$, and so do the ascending ones.

::: def
[Definition 6.2 — Morse–Smale functions and complexes]{.tag} $f$ is **Morse–Smale** if every ascending manifold meets every descending manifold transversally. The **Morse–Smale complex** has as cells the connected components of the sets
$$
D(p) \cap A(q), \quad p, q \text{ critical}.
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.3 — The Morse–Smale complex of a surface]{.tag} On a closed surface, let $f$ be Morse–Smale with $m_0$ minima, $m_1$ saddles and $m_2$ maxima.

-   Each saddle has four **separatrices**: two integral lines descending to minima and two ascending to maxima.
-   Each 2-cell is a quadrangle with corners minimum, saddle, maximum, saddle (Edelsbrunner, Harer and Zomorodian, 2003).
-   There are $4 m_1$ arcs and $2 m_1$ quadrangles.

::: proof
The two first statements follow from the local model of a saddle and from the transversality of the flow (EHZ 2003).

For the counts, each arc is a separatrix and has exactly one saddle end, which gives $4 m_1$ arcs. Each quadrangle has two saddle corners, and each saddle is a corner of the four sectors between its separatrices. Hence $2 \times \#\text{quadrangles} = 4 m_1$.

Euler's formula on this cell decomposition then reads
$$
(m_0 + m_1 + m_2) - 4 m_1 + 2 m_1 = m_0 - m_1 + m_2 = \chi(M),
$$
which is Theorem 3.4 again. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For $\cos 2\pi x + \cos 2\pi y$ on the torus, $m = (1, 2, 1)$: the complex has 4 nodes, 8 arcs and 4 quadrangles.

### 6.2 Watersheds

The ascending manifolds $A(m)$ of the minima are the **catchment basins** of $f$: the points whose steepest descent ends at $m$. Their boundaries form the **watershed** used in image segmentation (Vincent and Soille, 1991). Symmetrically, the descending manifolds $D(M)$ of the maxima of an image are the regions that climb to each bright peak.

On a grid, steepest ascent replaces the gradient: each pixel points to its highest neighbour, and the regions are the trees of these pointers. Each local maximum then has a region, and noise makes hundreds of them.

### 6.3 Discrete Morse–Smale complexes

Integrating integral lines numerically is fragile at saddles. The discrete gradients of Section 3.3 replace them: $V$-paths from critical edges to critical vertices are the descending separatrices, and dual paths to critical triangles the ascending ones. Gyulassy, Bremer, Hamann and Pascucci (2008) and Shivashankar and Natarajan (2012) compute such complexes in 3D and in parallel; TTK implements them.

### 6.4 Persistence-driven simplification

A saddle and an adjacent extremum connected by a single separatrix can be **cancelled**: the two critical points disappear, and the cells on both sides merge. Cancelling pairs in increasing order of persistence gives a hierarchy of Morse–Smale complexes (Edelsbrunner, Harer and Zomorodian, 2003).

In terms of regions, cancelling a maximum with the saddle where it meets an older peak merges its region into the older one. This is exactly the elder rule of Proposition 4.3, applied with a threshold $\tau$.

::: ex
[Code 6.1 — Segmentation by simplified descending manifolds]{.tag} On the noisy image of Code 4.2, steepest ascent assigns each pixel to a maximum. Whenever two regions meet at a pixel $v$ and the lower peak exceeds $f(v)$ by less than $\tau$, the lower region merges into the higher one. The result is compared with the regions of the clean image.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score

def segment(f, tau):
    """Descending manifolds of the maxima of f on the 4-neighbour grid, by steepest
    ascent, with the regions of maxima of persistence < tau merged (elder rule)."""
    n, m = f.shape
    flat = f.ravel()
    parent = -np.ones(n * m, dtype=int)
    def find(a):
        while parent[a] != a:
            parent[a] = parent[parent[a]]
            a = parent[a]
        return a
    for v in np.argsort(-flat, kind="stable"):          # decreasing values
        i, j = divmod(v, m)
        nb = [a * m + b for a, b in [(i - 1, j), (i + 1, j), (i, j - 1), (i, j + 1)]
              if 0 <= a < n and 0 <= b < m and parent[a * m + b] >= 0]
        if not nb:
            parent[v] = v                               # a new maximum
            continue
        parent[v] = find(max(nb, key=lambda u: flat[u]))  # steepest ascent
        for u in nb:
            ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
            if ru != rv and flat[v] > min(flat[ru], flat[rv]) - tau:   # low persistence
                young, old = (ru, rv) if flat[ru] < flat[rv] else (rv, ru)
                parent[young] = old
    return np.array([find(v) for v in range(n * m)]).reshape(n, m)

n = 64
x, y = np.meshgrid(np.arange(n), np.arange(n), indexing="ij")
bump = lambda cx, cy, h: h * np.exp(-((x - cx) ** 2 + (y - cy) ** 2) / (2 * 6.0 ** 2))
clean = bump(16, 16, 1.0) + bump(44, 20, 0.8) + bump(30, 48, 0.6)
img = clean + 0.05 * np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=(n, n))
truth = segment(clean, 0.0)
for tau in [0.0, 0.1, 0.25]:
    lab = segment(img, tau)
    ari = adjusted_rand_score(truth.ravel(), lab.ravel())
    print(f"tau = {tau:.2f}: {len(np.unique(lab)):3d} regions, "
          f"adjusted Rand index with the clean segmentation {ari:.3f}")
print("clean image:", len(np.unique(truth)), "regions")
```

The clean image has 3 regions. On the noisy image, $\tau = 0$ gives 721 regions (adjusted Rand index 0.008), $\tau = 0.1$ gives 66 (0.337), and $\tau = 0.25$, chosen in the gap of Code 4.2, gives 3 regions (0.844).
:::

The remaining disagreement lies in the flat background, where noise moves the boundaries.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 6

-   Integral lines of the gradient partition the domain into ascending and descending manifolds; their intersections form the Morse–Smale complex.
-   On a surface, every cell is a quadrangle, and there are $4 m_1$ arcs and $2 m_1$ cells.
-   Catchment basins are the ascending manifolds of minima; regions of bright features are the descending manifolds of maxima.
-   Discrete gradients compute these complexes exactly; cancelling pairs by persistence simplifies them, which removes the over-segmentation due to noise.
:::

## 7. Topological inference in high dimensions {#ch7}

A point cloud in $\mathbb{R}^{100}$ cannot be looked at, but its homology can be estimated. This chapter gives conditions under which the homology of a sampled shape is recovered, bounds the effect of noise and outliers, and turns persistence into a clustering algorithm.

### 7.1 Offsets, reach and sampling

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Medial axis and reach]{.tag} The **medial axis** of a compact set $K \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ is the set of points with at least two nearest points in $K$. The **reach** $\tau(K)$ is the distance from $K$ to its medial axis (Federer, 1959).
:::

A circle of radius $R$ has reach $R$: its medial axis is the centre. The boundary of a square has reach 0, since its medial axis, the diagonals, reaches the corners. Closed smooth submanifolds have positive reach.

::: thm
[Theorem 7.2 — Sampling theorem (Niyogi, Smale and Weinberger, 2008)]{.tag} Let $M \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a compact submanifold of reach $\tau$, and $X \subset M$ a finite set with $M \subseteq X^{\varepsilon / 2}$. If
$$
\varepsilon < \sqrt{3/5}\; \tau ,
$$
then $X^\varepsilon$ deformation retracts onto $M$. Consequently, $\check C(X, \varepsilon)$ has the homology of $M$.
:::
